name: Tesamorelin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2010 after two randomized, placebo-controlled trials in more than 800 adults with HIV, each lasting 26 weeks with a 26-week extension. The approval covers one narrow use: reducing excess belly fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
summary: A daily injection that prompts the pituitary to release growth hormone, approved to shrink excess belly fat in adults with HIV-related lipodystrophy.
keyTakeaway: Tesamorelin is a lab-made copy of the brain hormone that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. The FDA approved it in 2010, sold as Egrifta, to reduce deep belly fat in adults with HIV who have lipodystrophy. In the pivotal trials, fat around the organs fell by about 15 to 20% against placebo over six months, while body weight barely changed. The fat returned when treatment stopped. The label does not cover weight loss or general anti-aging use, and the drug is banned in sport.

blocks.text: Tesamorelin is a synthetic version of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), a 44-amino-acid peptide made by the hypothalamus, the small region at the base of the brain that controls the pituitary gland [2]. It is the active ingredient in Egrifta, a prescription medicine made by Theratechnologies [1].

Its one approved job is narrow: reducing the deep abdominal fat that builds up in some people with HIV who take antiretroviral therapy, a condition called lipodystrophy (an abnormal redistribution of body fat) [1]. The label is explicit that it is not a weight loss drug, since its effect on body weight is neutral [1].

In the 2000s, older HIV drug regimens left many patients with a thick waist and fat packed around the organs, even when the rest of the body grew thinner. Growth hormone itself was known to shrink this fat but carried side effects, so researchers tested a GHRH analog that would raise the body's own growth hormone in its natural pulses instead [2].

blocks.text: Tesamorelin binds the GHRH receptor on cells in the pituitary called somatotrophs, and in lab tests it does so about as strongly as the body's own hormone [1]. Those cells respond by making and releasing growth hormone in pulses. Growth hormone breaks down stored fat and builds tissue, and many of its effects run through IGF-1, a growth factor produced mainly by the liver [1].

This is an indirect route. Rather than supplying growth hormone from outside, tesamorelin turns up the body's own production, so the normal feedback loops that limit growth hormone stay in place. In the trials, IGF-1 rose by about two thirds over six months, a gain of roughly 105 to 120 ng/mL more than with placebo [1].

The fat loss falls mostly on visceral adipose tissue, the fat stored deep in the abdomen around the organs, rather than on the fat just under the skin [1][2]. Trunk fat fell by about 1 kg and lean mass rose by about 1.2 to 1.3 kg, while total weight hardly moved [1].

Yes. Tesamorelin was first approved in the United States in 2010 [1]. The most recent version, Egrifta WR, was approved in March 2025 and replaces Egrifta SV; the two use different vial strengths and mixing steps and cannot be swapped for each other [1].

The approval is limited to adults with HIV and lipodystrophy who carry excess abdominal fat [1]. Use for general weight loss, body building, or anti-aging falls outside the label, and the long-term effect on heart health has not been established [1]. Clinics that prescribe compounded tesamorelin for other purposes are working outside the approval.

Tesamorelin is prescribed to reduce excess visceral fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy [1]. The two pivotal trials enrolled 816 adults aged 18 to 65 on stable antiretroviral therapy, randomized two to one to a daily injection or placebo for 26 weeks, with fat measured by CT scan at the lower spine [1].

The benefit depends on staying on treatment. When people who responded were switched to placebo for the next 26 weeks, their visceral fat climbed back by 16 to 22% in that time, while those who stayed on the drug kept their reduction [1]. The second trial's authors also reported less distress about body image [2].

Outside the label, a randomized trial in 61 people with HIV and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease found that a year of tesamorelin cut liver fat by about a third relative to baseline, and 35% reached normal liver fat compared with 4% on placebo [3]. That finding has not led to a new approved use.

Most side effects trace back to higher growth hormone levels, which cause the body to hold more fluid. Joint pain, limb pain, swelling of the legs, muscle aches, and tingling or numbness all occurred more often with tesamorelin than with placebo [1].

items: Injection site reactions such as redness and itching: 25% versus 14% on placebo [1]
Muscle pain and leg swelling: 6% each versus 2% [1]
Allergic reactions such as rash and hives: 4% [1]

blocks.text: Blood sugar can rise. In the trials, 5% of tesamorelin users reached an HbA1c (a three-month average of blood sugar) of 6.5% or higher, against 1% on placebo, so glucose is checked before and during treatment [1]. The label also calls for monitoring IGF-1, since the long-term effect of persistently high levels is unknown [1].

The drug is not used during pregnancy, in people with active cancer, or in people whose hypothalamic-pituitary system has been damaged by surgery, radiation, or disease [1]. About half of trial patients developed antibodies to tesamorelin within six months, though those with and without antibodies saw similar fat reductions [1].
For athletes, tesamorelin is named on the World Anti-Doping Agency list as a GHRH analog and is prohibited in and out of competition [4].
